analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes entirely.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee after its referral.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the federal estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax, so that inherited wealth and large gifts would no longer face any federal tax. It applied to deaths and transfers after enactment. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of very large estates and receivers of large gifts — the tax applies only to transfers well above typical family wealth — plus wealthy families planning how to pass assets to the next generation.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Subtitle B of the Internal Revenue Code, which contains the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax, eliminating any federal tax on those transfers [S3].
The repeal applies to estates of people dying and transfers made after the act is enacted, so heirs of large estates would pay nothing on inheritances from that point on [S3].
The CRS summary confirms the bill repeals the estate tax, gift tax, and tax on generation-skipping transfers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, since the bill provides no replacement revenue. The estate and gift taxes fall almost entirely on the largest transfers of wealth, so the revenue they raise would be lost, leaving other taxpayers or future spending cuts to absorb the difference.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the taxes outright with no replacement revenue, so the money the estate and gift taxes raise would simply disappear from the federal budget [S3].

Because the estate tax applies only to the largest estates, the benefit is concentrated among the wealthiest families, while the lost revenue is borne broadly by everyone who pays federal taxes — a distribution most tax analysts describe as heavily tilted toward the top.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go almost entirely to heirs of very large estates, while the cost — lost federal revenue with no offset — is spread across all taxpayers. For anyone not inheriting a multi-million-dollar estate, the bill offers no direct benefit and a share of the fiscal cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Klink introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, the first day of the 106th Congress [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — so the bill died in committee when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the estate and gift taxes stayed in place and the federal government kept the revenue they raise; the heirs of large estates did not get the repeal they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broad taxpayers kept the estate-tax revenue

for.name: Rep. Ron Klink
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate and gift taxes on the opening day of the 106th Congress.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled any action on it.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no party split is on record; the sponsorship was small and bipartisan — one Democrat and one Republican.

industries.note: The bill would have eliminated the only federal tax on inherited wealth; because it did not pass, the largest estates remain subject to the estate tax. Its benefit would have flowed almost entirely to the top of the wealth distribution.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and wealth advisors
industries.note: Full repeal would have eliminated much of the demand for estate-tax planning work. The bill died, so the industry's business continues.
